I could not join the call on Tuesday. What did the buyer say?
Their lawyer stated that they wanted two hundred thousand credits, but only if the credits were issued by the end of March.
March? That is tight. Did the verifier say anything about the report?
He confirmed that the map annex had arrived, and he noted that the discrepancy was still under review.
So nobody promised a date.
No. And our finance director warned that the price might fall before the spring. He argued that we should not accept a fixed price.
How did the buyer react to that?
Their lawyer acknowledged that the market was moving, but she said a fixed price was not negotiable.
So where did it end?
I pointed out that we could not control the verification date, and I advised them to link the payment to the issuance, not to a date. They said they would send a draft by Friday.

Before we close, let me summarize where we are, so that nobody leaves with a different version. First, the decision. We agree in principle to buy two hundred thousand credits from the Serra Verde project, subject to verification. Second, the objection. Your finance director has argued that a fixed price exposes you if the market falls, and I have noted that. Our position has not changed. We need a fixed price, because our board approves budgets a year in advance. Third, the next step. Amanda has proposed linking the payment to the date the credits are issued, instead of a calendar date. I think that could work, but I cannot confirm it today. We will send a draft clause by Friday, and I would ask you to send your comments within a week. If anyone remembers this differently, please say so now.

When you report what somebody said in a meeting, the verb you choose is not a detail. It is a decision, and the reader will trust it. Said is neutral, and neutral is often the safest choice. But the other verbs carry information. If you write that the other side argued something, you are telling the reader that they gave reasons and that somebody disagreed. If you write that they acknowledged something, you are saying they accepted a point they did not like, and that is useful to know. And then there is claimed. Claimed means you are not sure the statement is true. In your own notes that may be fine. In an email that the other side will read, it is close to an accusation. So before you send the summary, read only the verbs. If the verbs tell a story that you would not say out loud in the room, change them.

Start by saying which meeting it was, and who was there. Then report the decision. Then report the objection, and who raised it. Then report the next step, and who owns it. And finally, say what is still open.
